The middle leg of the triangular trade carrying rum from New England to Africa
The brutal ocean voyage transporting enslaved Africans to the Americas
The colonial coastal shipping route between the Chesapeake and the New England ports
quiz.e: The Middle Passage was the deadly transatlantic voyage that forcibly transported enslaved Africans.

quiz.q: The House of Burgesses (1619) is significant as:
o: The first colonial court system with authority to overturn the royal governor
The first religious assembly to set church policy in the English colonies
The first representative legislative assembly in English America
The first town council to be chosen by all free adult colonists
quiz.e: Established in Virginia, it was the first elected representative body in the English colonies.

quiz.q: Why did South Carolina rely heavily on enslaved labor for rice cultivation?
o: Planters were required by law to use enslaved labor on all rice plantations
Rice was a low-cost crop that needed little labor and few workers
Enslaved Africans brought rice-growing expertise from West Africa
Native peoples already grew rice and taught planters to cultivate it
quiz.e: Many enslaved Africans came from rice-growing regions of West Africa and brought valuable agricultural expertise.

quiz.q: Colonial slave codes in Virginia (1660s-1705) established slavery as:
o: Temporary and reversible
Lifelong, hereditary, and race-based
Optional for enslaved individuals
Limited to non-Christians only
quiz.e: These codes codified slavery as a permanent, hereditary, racially defined status.

quiz.q: Which of these was a defining feature of New England town life?
o: Large plantations worked by enslaved laborers and governed by wealthy landowners
Scattered farms on frontier land and an Anglican parish system
Town meetings and Congregationalist church governance
Rapid growth of cash crops and a reliance on indentured servants
quiz.e: New England towns centered on Congregationalist churches and relatively democratic town meetings.

quiz.q: The triangular trade linked which three regions?
o: Europe, Africa, and the Americas
Asia, Europe, and Africa
North America, South America, and Asia
England, France, and Spain
quiz.e: Manufactured goods, enslaved Africans, and raw materials/cash crops circulated among Europe, Africa, and the Americas.

quiz.q: Roger Williams founded Rhode Island primarily to promote:
o: Strict enforcement of Puritan religious law and a church-run government
A profitable trading colony and a proprietary grant to wealthy investors
Religious toleration and separation of church and state
A refuge for English Catholics and a ban on dissenting Protestants
quiz.e: Williams, banished from Massachusetts Bay, founded Rhode Island on principles of religious freedom and separation of church/state.

quiz.q: By the mid-1700s, the population of the Lower South was increasingly:
o: Majority enslaved African in some areas
Entirely composed of indentured servants
Free of any slave labor
Majority Native American
quiz.e: Enslaved Africans formed the majority population in parts of the Lower South by the mid-18th century due to plantation agriculture.

quiz.q: The Albany Congress (1754) proposed the Albany Plan of Union, which:
o: Was a successful agreement that bound the colonies to Britain's wartime leadership
Won approval from every colonial assembly but was vetoed by the Crown
Was an early, ultimately rejected step toward colonial cooperation
Created a permanent colonial army and gave Parliament direct taxing power
quiz.e: Franklin's plan for colonial unity was rejected by the colonies but foreshadowed later cooperative efforts.

quiz.q: The Proclamation of 1763 angered colonists because it:
o: Placed a tax on all printed documents sold in the colonies
Forbade settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains
Required colonists to house and supply British troops in their homes
Banned colonial trade with France and Spain's Caribbean colonies
quiz.e: The Proclamation restricted westward expansion, frustrating land-hungry colonists after the costly war.

quiz.q: The phrase 'no taxation without representation' arose in protest of:
o: The Stamp Act
The Emancipation Proclamation
The Missouri Compromise
The Wagner Act
quiz.e: Colonists protested the Stamp Act (1765) as illegitimate direct taxation without their consent via Parliament.

quiz.q: John Locke's philosophy directly influenced the Declaration of Independence through the concept of:
o: The divine right of kings and loyalty to a hereditary monarch
Mercantilist regulation of colonial trade for the benefit of Britain
Natural rights (life, liberty, property) and government by consent
Separation of powers and a strong executive with lifetime tenure
quiz.e: Locke's natural rights and social contract theory underpin Jefferson's arguments in the Declaration.

quiz.q: The main weakness of the Articles of Confederation was:
o: Lack of power to tax or maintain a standing army
A powerful national judiciary and an executive able to veto state laws
Equal state representation and a requirement of unanimity to amend
Excessive federal control over state militias and local trade policy
quiz.e: The Articles created a deliberately weak national government with no power to tax or field an army, crippling its effectiveness.

quiz.q: Shays' Rebellion (1786-87) demonstrated:
o: The Confederation government's success in raising troops and putting down unrest
The Confederation government's inability to maintain order or raise funds
Widespread farmer support for restoring the British monarchy in Massachusetts
The need for a bill of rights to protect citizens from state governments
quiz.e: The armed uprising of indebted farmers showed the Confederation government could not effectively respond to internal unrest.

quiz.q: The Three-Fifths Compromise addressed:
o: Representation and taxation counting of enslaved people
Representation and taxation of slaves in the Senate and Electoral College
How states would share western lands and the national war debt
The rules for admitting new states and ending the foreign slave trade
quiz.e: It counted enslaved people as 3/5 of a person for apportioning representatives and direct taxes.

quiz.q: The Great (Connecticut) Compromise created:
o: A one-house legislature with representation based on each state's wealth and size
A two-house legislature with both chambers based on state population alone
A bicameral legislature with the House based on population and Senate with equal representation
A legislature where states held equal votes and the executive chosen by Congress
quiz.e: The compromise balanced large and small state interests via a bicameral Congress.

quiz.q: Anti-Federalists opposed ratifying the Constitution mainly because:
o: They believed the Constitution gave too little power to the national government to defend the states
They feared a strong central government would threaten individual liberties without a bill of rights
They hoped to keep the Articles but wanted a stronger president elected for life
They worried that large states would be overrepresented and demanded annual elections
quiz.e: Anti-Federalists feared federal overreach and demanded a bill of rights to protect individual liberties.

quiz.q: Hamilton's financial plan included all of the following EXCEPT:
o: A national bank
Federal assumption of state debts
Protective tariffs
Abolition of the national debt
quiz.e: Hamilton's plan managed and consolidated debt rather than abolishing it; it included a bank, debt assumption, and tariffs.

quiz.q: The Whiskey Rebellion (1794) is significant because Washington's response demonstrated:
o: The federal government's willingness and ability to enforce its authority
The federal government's reluctance to use force against citizens protesting taxes
Washington's support for the farmers' grievances over the excise tax
That state militias, not federal troops, were responsible for enforcing national laws
quiz.e: Washington used federal troops to suppress the tax revolt, asserting federal authority under the new Constitution.

quiz.q: Common Sense by Thomas Paine argued primarily for:
o: Reconciliation with Britain
American independence and against monarchy
Continued colonial loyalty to the king
A return to salutary neglect
quiz.e: Paine's widely read pamphlet made a persuasive, accessible case for independence and republican government.

quiz.q: The Northwest Ordinance (1787) was significant because it:
o: Set up the first national bank and a uniform currency for the western territories
Gave the president power to appoint territorial governors and extend slavery
Granted Native peoples permanent title to their lands north of the Ohio River
Established a process for territories to become states and banned slavery in the Northwest Territory
quiz.e: It provided an orderly path to statehood and prohibited slavery in the territory, one of the Confederation's few successes.

quiz.q: The first American political party system emerged over disagreements between:
o: Adams's Whigs and Jackson's Democrats over the national bank and expansion
Hamilton's Republicans and Jefferson's Federalists over a state-run economy
Hamilton's Federalists and Jefferson's Democratic-Republicans
Northern Federalists and Southern Democrats over the extension of slavery
quiz.e: Hamilton (strong federal government, loose construction) and Jefferson (states' rights, strict construction) led opposing early parties.

quiz.q: The Bill of Rights was added to the Constitution primarily to:
o: Secure ratification by protecting individual liberties from federal overreach
Give the federal government clearer taxing power and a national army
Guarantee equal representation for small states in both houses of Congress
End the foreign slave trade and give the president control of foreign policy
quiz.e: Anti-Federalist concerns about a lack of explicit rights protections led to the Bill of Rights as a condition for broader support.

quiz.q: Jacksonian Democracy expanded political participation primarily for:
o: All white men and women who owned land or paid taxes in their states
Free Black men and Native Americans through new state constitutions
White men, through the removal of property requirements for voting
Wealthy planters and merchants through reduced property qualifications for office
quiz.e: Suffrage expansion under Jackson applied to white men; Native Americans and enslaved people faced increased exclusion/oppression.

quiz.q: The Indian Removal Act (1830) led directly to:
o: The Missouri Compromise
The Trail of Tears
The Nullification Crisis
The Bank War
quiz.e: The Act authorized forced relocation of tribes like the Cherokee, resulting in the deadly Trail of Tears.

quiz.q: The Erie Canal's completion (1825) primarily contributed to:
o: Opening the Mississippi River to American shipping and doubling the nation's size
Ending the dominance of the National Bank over western land sales
Linking the Great Lakes region to Atlantic trade, boosting the Market Revolution
Connecting the Ohio Valley to the Gulf of Mexico and the cotton South
quiz.e: The canal connected western agricultural regions to Eastern markets, a key part of the Market Revolution.

quiz.q: The Second Great Awakening most directly fueled which reform movement?
o: Abolitionism
Mercantilism
Nullification
Manifest Destiny
quiz.e: Religious revivalism's emphasis on human perfectibility and moral action fueled abolitionist and other reform movements.

quiz.q: The Seneca Falls Convention (1848) is best known for:
o: Founding the first anti-slavery society and demanding immediate emancipation
Passing a state law that gave married women property rights
Winning women the right to vote through the Nineteenth Amendment
Launching the organized women's rights movement with the Declaration of Sentiments
quiz.e: The convention, led by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, produced the Declaration of Sentiments demanding women's rights.

quiz.q: The Wilmot Proviso (1846) proposed to:
o: Ban slavery in territory won from Mexico
Expand slavery into all new territories
Abolish slavery nationwide
End the Mexican-American War
quiz.e: Though it never passed, the Proviso's proposal to ban slavery in Mexican Cession territory intensified sectional tensions.

quiz.q: The Lowell System employed primarily:
o: Enslaved laborers
Young unmarried women in textile mills
Native American workers
Formerly indentured servants
quiz.e: The Lowell mills in Massachusetts employed young women under close supervision, an early industrial wage-labor model.

quiz.q: Jackson's veto of the Second Bank of the United States reflected his view that the bank:
o: Was an elite monopoly harming ordinary Americans
Was too weak to control inflation
Should be expanded, not eliminated
Was unconstitutional under the Bill of Rights
quiz.e: Jackson saw the Bank as favoring wealthy elites and vetoed its re-charter as part of the 'Bank War.'

quiz.q: The Nullification Crisis (1832-33) centered on South Carolina's claim that:
o: The federal government had no authority to charge any tariff on imports
Congress lacked the power to admit new slave states to the Union
States held the right to secede from the Union at will over slavery
States could nullify federal laws (the tariff) they deemed unconstitutional
quiz.e: South Carolina argued it could nullify the federal tariff, testing the balance of federal versus state power.

quiz.q: William Lloyd Garrison's The Liberator advocated for:
o: Gradual, compensated emancipation
Immediate abolition of slavery
Colonization of freed slaves to Africa
Expansion of slavery westward
quiz.e: Garrison was a leading voice for the immediate, uncompensated abolition of slavery.

quiz.q: Manifest Destiny is best defined as:
o: A treaty with Britain that set the northern border of the Oregon Country
A congressional compromise that admitted new states as free or slave
The belief that American expansion across the continent was inevitable and divinely sanctioned
A diplomatic doctrine warning European powers to stay out of the Americas
quiz.e: Manifest Destiny was the widely held ideological justification for continental American expansion.

quiz.q: The Mexican Cession resulted from:
o: The Louisiana Purchase
The Mexican-American War (1846-48)
The War of 1812
The Missouri Compromise
quiz.e: The U.S. victory in the Mexican-American War brought California and the New Mexico territory into U.S. possession.

quiz.q: Which best characterizes the antebellum middle class ideal of womanhood, or 'cult of domesticity'?
o: Women should share equally with men in business and politics outside the home
Women were naturally suited to wage labor in the new mill towns
Women's proper sphere was the home, as moral guardians of the family
Women should advance reform by lecturing and petitioning for suffrage
quiz.e: As industrial work moved outside the home, a new ideology idealized women's role within domestic, moral spheres.

quiz.q: Jefferson's Louisiana Purchase (1803) created a constitutional dilemma because:
o: The Constitution gave the president no power to negotiate treaties with foreign nations
Jefferson was a strict constructionist but the purchase required a loose interpretation of federal power
Congress rejected the purchase and Jefferson acted without its consent
Spain and France disputed ownership, delaying the transfer for years
quiz.e: Jefferson, who favored strict construction, had to stretch his constitutional views to justify the purchase's constitutionality.

quiz.q: Horace Mann's education reforms primarily promoted:
o: Private religious schools only
Common (public) schools accessible to all children
The abolition of universities
Military academies
quiz.e: Mann championed the common school movement, advocating for free, publicly funded education.

quiz.q: The Compromise of 1850 included all of the following EXCEPT:
o: California admitted as a free state
A stronger Fugitive Slave Act
Popular sovereignty in Utah and New Mexico territories
Immediate abolition of slavery nationwide
quiz.e: The Compromise did not abolish slavery; it balanced free/slave state admission and strengthened fugitive slave enforcement.

quiz.q: The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) is significant because it:
o: Extended the Missouri Compromise line westward and banned slavery north of it
Admitted Kansas as a free state and Nebraska as a slave state
Settled the dispute over slavery by letting Congress decide each territory's status
Repealed the Missouri Compromise line by introducing popular sovereignty, leading to 'Bleeding Kansas'
quiz.e: By allowing territories to vote on slavery, the Act effectively nullified the Missouri Compromise and caused violent conflict.

quiz.q: The Dred Scott v. Sandford decision (1857) ruled that:
o: Black Americans were citizens, but Congress could still restrict slavery in territories
Slavery was illegal in free states, so Scott's residence there made him free
States could refuse to return fugitives, and Congress must protect free soil
Enslaved people were not citizens, and Congress could not ban slavery in territories
quiz.e: The ruling denied Black citizenship and struck down congressional power to restrict slavery in territories, inflaming the North.

quiz.q: The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) applied to:
o: All enslaved people in the United States, including border states
Enslaved people only in Confederate-held territory
Only enslaved people in Washington, D.C.
No one immediately, only a future promise
quiz.e: It freed enslaved people in Confederate territory only, not in the loyal border states, as a wartime measure.

quiz.q: Which battle is considered the war's turning point that also enabled the Emancipation Proclamation?
o: Fort Sumter
Antietam
Appomattox
Bull Run
quiz.e: The Union's tactical success (or at least non-defeat) at Antietam (1862) gave Lincoln the opening to issue the Proclamation.

quiz.q: The 14th Amendment (1868) is best known for establishing:
o: Birthright citizenship and equal protection under the law
Voting rights for Black men and the end of poll taxes and literacy tests
A ban on slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States
Voting rights for women and the direct election of senators
quiz.e: The 14th Amendment granted citizenship to all born in the U.S. and guaranteed equal protection of the laws.

quiz.q: The Freedmen's Bureau provided which service during Reconstruction?
o: Land, tools, and mules to all freedpeople, taken from former Confederate plantations
Federal troops to protect Black voters at polling places throughout the North
Loans to Southern planters to rebuild their farms with paid free labor
Education, food, and legal aid to formerly enslaved people
quiz.e: The Bureau assisted freedpeople with education, basic necessities, and legal support after emancipation.

quiz.q: The Compromise of 1877 resulted in:
o: Hayes securing the presidency in exchange for withdrawing federal troops from the South
Tilden taking the presidency in exchange for strengthening the Freedmen's Bureau
The Senate removing Johnson from office and ending Reconstruction in the South
Congress sending more federal troops to enforce Black voting rights in the South
quiz.e: The disputed 1876 election was resolved by giving Hayes the presidency while ending federal enforcement of Reconstruction in the South.

quiz.q: Sharecropping after the Civil War primarily:
o: Gave freedpeople a path to owning their own land after a few years of labor
Freed Southern farmers from crop liens and gave them fair prices for cotton
Trapped many freedpeople in cycles of debt and economic dependency
Led to the rapid growth of small independent Black-owned farms across the South
quiz.e: Sharecropping often left freedpeople indebted to landowners, replicating economic subordination in a new form.

quiz.q: Radical Republicans in Congress pushed Reconstruction policies that were generally:
o: More forgiving of former Confederate leaders than Lincoln's or Johnson's plans
Aimed mainly at rebuilding Southern railroads and restoring cotton exports
Stricter and more protective of freedpeople's rights than Lincoln's or Johnson's plans
Dedicated to restoring state governments quickly with few conditions on the South
quiz.e: Radical Republicans favored stronger federal protections for freedpeople than the more lenient presidential Reconstruction plans.

quiz.q: Which event most directly triggered Southern secession?
o: The Emancipation Proclamation
Abraham Lincoln's election in 1860
The Missouri Compromise
The Compromise of 1850
quiz.e: Lincoln's election as a sectional, anti-slavery-expansion candidate prompted South Carolina and other states to secede.

quiz.q: Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) had which effect on the nation?
o: It calmed sectional tensions
It galvanized Northern anti-slavery sentiment
It ended the fugitive slave laws
It was banned throughout the North
quiz.e: Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel intensified Northern opposition to slavery and heightened sectional conflict.

quiz.q: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) legalized which doctrine?
o: 'Separate but equal' racial segregation
Full racial integration
Abolition of Jim Crow laws
Universal male suffrage
quiz.e: The ruling upheld legal segregation under the 'separate but equal' doctrine, a legacy that outlasted Reconstruction.

quiz.q: Which factor most reduced Northern political will to enforce Reconstruction by the mid-1870s?
o: A constitutional amendment banning Reconstruction
War-weariness and the economic Panic of 1873
A Supreme Court ruling ending Reconstruction immediately
Southern reunification with full racial equality
quiz.e: Economic troubles and general war-weariness eroded Northern commitment to continued federal enforcement in the South.

quiz.q: The 15th Amendment (1870) specifically addressed:
o: Abolition of slavery
Birthright citizenship
The right to vote regardless of race
Equal protection under the law
quiz.e: The 15th Amendment barred denying voting rights based on race, though it left loopholes later exploited by Jim Crow laws.

quiz.q: Which advantage did the Union have over the Confederacy at the start of the Civil War?
o: A larger population and greater industrial capacity
Superior military leadership in every battle
Home-field defensive advantage
International recognition from Britain and France
quiz.e: The Union's larger population and industrial base were long-term structural advantages over the agrarian Confederacy.

quiz.q: Andrew Carnegie's steel empire is a classic example of:
o: Horizontal integration
Vertical integration
Free trade policy
Populism
quiz.e: Carnegie controlled every stage of steel production, from raw materials to finished product — vertical integration.

quiz.q: John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil primarily grew through:
o: Horizontal integration (buying out competitors)
Vertical integration, owning every stage from raw materials to final sale
Large federal contracts and tariff protections granted by Congress
Innovative new refining techniques that no competitor could imitate
quiz.e: Rockefeller consolidated the oil industry by acquiring and merging with competing companies.

quiz.q: Social Darwinism was used in the Gilded Age to justify:
o: Wealth inequality and opposition to government regulation of business
Government regulation of railroads and protection of workers from harsh conditions
Reforms to break up monopolies and redistribute wealth to the poor
Public spending on housing and education for urban immigrants
quiz.e: Applying 'survival of the fittest' to society, Social Darwinism rationalized inequality and minimal business regulation.

quiz.q: The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) was significant as:
o: The first law to bar all immigrants from Asia and set a nationwide quota system
A law passed in response to Chinese violence against American workers
The first major U.S. law restricting immigration by nationality
A federal law ending the labor contract system that brought Chinese workers
quiz.e: It was the first major federal law to exclude immigrants specifically based on national origin.

quiz.q: Political machines like Tammany Hall provided immigrants with:
o: Public housing and pensions funded by federal programs for immigrant families
Practical services and jobs in exchange for votes, despite widespread corruption
Honest local government with citizens elected by fair, secret ballots
Legal protection from deportation in exchange for joining labor unions
quiz.e: Machines traded services and patronage jobs for political loyalty, functioning within a system rife with graft.

quiz.q: The Knights of Labor differed from the American Federation of Labor mainly by:
o: Focusing on skilled craft workers and negotiating better wages and hours
Organizing only industrial workers and calling for violent revolution
Welcoming all workers, including women and Black workers, and pursuing broad social reform
Excluding immigrants and favoring strikes over political reform
quiz.e: The Knights were broadly inclusive; the AFL (Gompers) focused narrowly on skilled workers' wages and hours.

quiz.q: The Haymarket Affair (1886) resulted in:
o: A public backlash against labor unions, linking them to radicalism
Public sympathy for workers and rapid growth in union membership nationwide
A court ruling that made all strikes legal and protected union leaders
The collapse of the Knights of Labor's leadership and new federal labor laws
quiz.e: The bombing at a Chicago labor rally caused a backlash that associated organized labor with anarchist violence.

quiz.q: The Populist Party's Omaha Platform (1892) called for all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Free coinage of silver
A graduated income tax
Direct election of senators
The gold standard
quiz.e: Populists favored free silver to expand the money supply, opposing the tight-money gold standard.

quiz.q: William Jennings Bryan's 'Cross of Gold' speech (1896) advocated for:
o: The gold standard to keep currency stable and protect eastern banks
Free silver to expand the money supply and ease farmer debt
Higher tariffs to protect American industry and raise wages for workers
Government ownership of railroads to lower shipping rates for farmers
quiz.e: Bryan championed free silver coinage to inflate currency and relieve indebted farmers, in his famous speech.

quiz.q: The transcontinental railroad (completed 1869) relied heavily on the labor of:
o: Enslaved African Americans
Chinese and Irish immigrants
Native American laborers exclusively
European aristocrats
quiz.e: Chinese immigrants (working west from California) and Irish immigrants (working east) provided crucial labor for the railroad.

quiz.q: The Bessemer process was significant because it:
o: Allowed cheap mass production of cotton cloth and expanded textile mills
Sped up railroad construction by creating a standard track gauge
Created new oil-refining methods that made kerosene widely affordable
Made steel production cheaper and more efficient, enabling industrial growth
quiz.e: The Bessemer process lowered steel production costs, fueling railroad expansion and industrial construction.

quiz.q: 'New immigrants' of the late 19th century primarily came from:
o: Northern and Western Europe
Southern and Eastern Europe
Latin America
East Asia exclusively
quiz.e: New immigrants from Italy, Poland, and Russia (including many Jews) differed culturally from earlier immigrant waves, fueling nativism.

quiz.q: The Social Gospel movement responded to industrial-era poverty by:
o: Urging the wealthy to leave the cities and fund farms for the poor
Teaching that poverty was a sign of moral weakness and personal failure
Supporting tough anti-immigration laws to protect city jobs and wages
Applying Christian ethics to social problems through action like settlement houses
quiz.e: The Social Gospel encouraged Christians to address social problems directly, exemplified by Jane Addams's Hull House.

quiz.q: The Homestead and Pullman strikes of the 1890s demonstrated that:
o: Government and the courts tended to sympathize with strikers and support unions
Workers could win strikes by using violence against company property
State legislatures passed laws that recognized the right to strike
Government and private security often sided with business against labor
quiz.e: Both strikes were suppressed by private security forces or federal troops, showing government's frequent alignment with business interests.

quiz.q: The Grange and Farmers' Alliances were precursors to which political movement?
o: Progressivism
Populism
Abolitionism
The Federalist Party
quiz.e: These farmer cooperative organizations evolved into the Populist (People's) Party in the 1890s.

quiz.q: Upton Sinclair's The Jungle is an example of:
o: Progressive political theory that argued for expanding the right to vote
Muckraking journalism that spurred food safety reform
Social Gospel preaching that called on churches to fund settlement houses
Social Darwinist writing that defended unregulated competition in industry
quiz.e: Sinclair's exposé of meatpacking conditions spurred passage of the Pure Food and Drug Act (1906).

quiz.q: The 17th Amendment established:
o: The right of women to vote in all federal and state elections
A national ban on the sale and manufacture of alcoholic beverages
Direct election of U.S. senators by voters
A federal tax on personal incomes to fund government spending
quiz.e: The 17th Amendment (1913) changed senator selection from state legislatures to direct popular election.

quiz.q: Theodore Roosevelt's approach to trusts under the 'Square Deal' was to:
o: Break up and eliminate all large corporations
Regulate rather than eliminate big business
Ignore corporate practices entirely
Nationalize all major industries
quiz.e: Roosevelt distinguished between 'good' and 'bad' trusts, pursuing regulation rather than universal dissolution of big business.

quiz.q: The Federal Reserve System, created in 1913, was designed to:
o: Provide a fixed gold-based currency and replace private banks entirely
Allow the president to set interest rates and control federal spending
Break up trusts and regulate industrial prices across the nation
Provide a stable, elastic national currency and oversee banking
quiz.e: Wilson's New Freedom created the Federal Reserve to stabilize the banking and monetary system.

quiz.q: The Spanish-American War (1898) resulted in U.S. acquisition of:
o: The Philippines, Puerto Rico, and Guam
Cuba, Hawaii, and the Samoan Islands as new territories
Cuba, Puerto Rico, and the Philippines as annexed states
The Philippines, Guam, and Hawaii as protectorates
quiz.e: The war's outcome gave the U.S. control of the Philippines, Puerto Rico, and Guam; Cuba became a protectorate.

quiz.q: The Zimmermann Telegram contributed to U.S. entry into WWI by:
o: Offering a German-American alliance against Britain in exchange for loans
Proposing a German-Mexican alliance against the U.S.
Announcing unrestricted submarine warfare against American merchant ships
Warning that Germany would invade Mexico unless the U.S. stayed neutral
quiz.e: The intercepted telegram revealed Germany's proposal to ally with Mexico against the U.S., inflaming American public opinion.

quiz.q: The U.S. Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles primarily due to opposition to:
o: Reparations imposed on Germany
U.S. membership in the League of Nations
The redrawing of European borders
Wilson's Fourteen Points
quiz.e: Senators feared League membership would entangle the U.S. in foreign conflicts, reflecting isolationist sentiment.

quiz.q: The Harlem Renaissance was centered on:
o: A movement that reformed city government and ended corrupt machine politics
A farm-based political movement that demanded credit for rural workers
A flourishing of African American art, literature, and music
A union drive among Black factory workers in the urban North
quiz.e: The Harlem Renaissance was a vibrant cultural movement of Black artists, writers, and musicians in 1920s New York.

quiz.q: The Scopes Trial (1925) centered on a conflict between:
o: Evolution and religious fundamentalism
Prohibition and temperance
Immigration and nativism
Labor and capital
quiz.e: The trial pitted the teaching of evolution against fundamentalist religious objections, reflecting 1920s cultural conflict.

quiz.q: The National Origins Act (1924) was designed to:
o: Open the country to more immigrants from Southern and Eastern Europe
Admit all immigrants with job skills regardless of national origin
Restrict immigration through quotas favoring Northern/Western Europe
Bar all Asian immigration and end the system of national quotas
quiz.e: The Act set nativist quotas that favored immigrants from Northern and Western Europe.

quiz.q: Which New Deal program provided retirement pensions and is still in effect today?
o: The Wagner Act
Social Security Act
The TVA
The FDIC
quiz.e: The Social Security Act (1935) established a retirement pension system, a lasting New Deal legacy.

quiz.q: The Wagner Act (1935) primarily:
o: Protected workers' rights to organize unions and engage in collective bargaining
Banned child labor and set a maximum workweek for industrial workers
Set a national minimum wage and a forty-hour work week
Created old-age pensions and unemployment insurance funded by payroll taxes
quiz.e: The Wagner Act guaranteed workers' rights to unionize and bargain collectively, a major pro-labor New Deal reform.

quiz.q: What ultimately ended the Great Depression?
o: The New Deal alone
World War II mobilization and full employment
The stock market recovery of 1932
The Social Security Act
quiz.e: Massive wartime spending and full employment during WWII, not the New Deal alone, finally ended the Depression.

quiz.q: Japanese American internment during WWII was based on:
o: Documented evidence that specific individuals had spied for Japan
Court findings that Japanese Americans had sabotaged defense plants
Ancestry alone, without individual evidence of wrongdoing
Requests by Japanese American community leaders for government protection
quiz.e: Executive Order 9066 forced relocation based solely on Japanese ancestry, later upheld in Korematsu but widely condemned since.

quiz.q: The Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine asserted the U.S. right to:
o: Intervene in Latin American affairs to maintain stability
Expand U.S. territory by annexing European colonies in the Caribbean
Withdraw from Latin American affairs and respect national sovereignty
Ban all European trade with the countries of Central America
quiz.e: The Corollary expanded the Monroe Doctrine, claiming U.S. authority to intervene in Latin America as an international police power.

quiz.q: The core U.S. Cold War strategy of containment aimed to:
o: Prevent the further spread of communism without direct war with the USSR
Roll back communism by supporting rebellions inside the Soviet Union
Trade freely with communist nations to encourage democratic reform
Reduce military spending and withdraw American troops from Europe
quiz.e: George Kennan's containment strategy sought to stop communism's spread through means short of direct war with the USSR.

quiz.q: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) ruled that:
o: Public school segregation was legal if facilities were equal in quality
Public schools had to desegregate immediately by mandatory busing
Segregation in all public places, including parks and restaurants, was unlawful
Public school segregation was unconstitutional, overturning Plessy v. Ferguson
quiz.e: The Court unanimously ruled that 'separate but equal' schools were inherently unequal, overturning Plessy.

quiz.q: The Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-56) was sparked by:
o: The murder of Emmett Till and the acquittal of his killers in Mississippi
A Supreme Court ruling that struck down segregation in public schools
Martin Luther King Jr.'s call for a national march on the capital
Rosa Parks's arrest for refusing to give up her bus seat
quiz.e: Rosa Parks's arrest triggered the boycott, which launched Martin Luther King Jr.'s civil rights leadership.

quiz.q: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 primarily banned discrimination in:
o: Housing and voting by race and ending literacy tests in the South
Public accommodations and employment based on race, sex, religion, or national origin
Schools and juries by race, as the Fourteenth Amendment required
Public accommodations and federal hiring by race, but not employment in private business
quiz.e: The Act outlawed discrimination in public accommodations and employment across several protected categories.

quiz.q: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 specifically:
o: Banned discrimination in public accommodations and private employment
Prohibited poll taxes in state and federal elections through a constitutional amendment
Eliminated literacy tests and authorized federal oversight of voter registration
Guaranteed equal housing opportunity and banned segregation in public schools
quiz.e: The Act removed discriminatory barriers like literacy tests and allowed federal oversight in discriminatory jurisdictions.

quiz.q: Lyndon Johnson's Great Society included which major program?
o: The New Deal
Medicare and Medicaid
The Marshall Plan
The Federal Reserve System
quiz.e: Medicare (elderly health coverage) and Medicaid (health coverage for the poor) were signature Great Society programs (1965).

quiz.q: The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964) is significant because it:
o: Declared war on North Vietnam after the attack on American troops in Saigon
Required the president to seek congressional approval before sending ground troops
Gave President Johnson broad authority to escalate military action without a formal declaration of war
Ordered the gradual withdrawal of American forces and the training of South Vietnamese troops
quiz.e: The resolution granted the president sweeping war powers in Vietnam without Congress formally declaring war.

quiz.q: The Tet Offensive (1968) is considered a turning point in the Vietnam War because:
o: It was a clear communist victory that quickly forced a U.S. military withdrawal
Though a communist victory on the ground, it increased public support for the war
Though a military setback for the communists, it undermined American public confidence in the war
It destroyed North Vietnam's army and led to peace talks within a few weeks
quiz.e: Despite being a military failure for North Vietnam/Viet Cong, Tet shocked American public opinion and eroded war support.

quiz.q: The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) was resolved through:
o: A military strike on Cuba, with the Soviets withdrawing their navy from the Caribbean
Negotiation, with the Soviets removing missiles from Cuba and a secret U.S. pledge on Turkey
An agreement in which the U.S. kept its missiles in Turkey and invaded Cuba
A United Nations vote that required both sides to withdraw weapons from Europe
quiz.e: The crisis ended via back-channel diplomacy, avoiding direct war while resolving the missile standoff.

quiz.q: The War Powers Act (1973) was a direct legacy of which conflict?
o: World War II
The Korean War
The Vietnam War
The Persian Gulf War
quiz.e: Congress passed the Act to limit presidential war-making power in response to the executive overreach seen during Vietnam.

quiz.q: Roe v. Wade (1973) established:
o: A constitutional right to abortion
The Equal Rights Amendment
Title IX protections
The right to contraception
quiz.e: The Supreme Court ruling recognized a constitutional right to abortion under the right to privacy.

quiz.q: The Watergate scandal ultimately led to:
o: President Nixon's impeachment and removal by the Senate
President Nixon's resignation in 1974
A constitutional amendment on presidential term limits
The end of the Vietnam War
quiz.e: Facing near-certain impeachment, Nixon resigned in August 1974 rather than face trial.

quiz.q: Détente under Nixon referred to:
o: A policy of building up nuclear weapons and confronting the USSR in the Third World
A treaty that ended the Vietnam War and established a military alliance with Moscow
A strategy of ending trade with China and isolating communist nations
A policy of easing Cold War tensions with the USSR and opening relations with China
quiz.e: Détente sought to reduce Cold War tensions through diplomacy, arms limitation talks, and new relations with Communist China.

quiz.q: 'Stagflation' in the 1970s refers to:
o: Simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment
Falling prices and high unemployment caused by weak consumer demand
Rising wages and low unemployment caused by a boom in manufacturing
Rapid inflation combined with strong job growth and rising productivity
quiz.e: Stagflation combined stagnant growth/high unemployment with high inflation, challenging conventional economic policy.

quiz.q: The shift toward 'Black Power' in the late 1960s reflected:
o: Satisfaction with legislative gains and support for nonviolent integration into mainstream society
A call to end the movement and return to local church-based organizing
A shift toward Southern conservatism and approval of gradual voting reform
Frustration with the pace of change and an emphasis on Black self-determination
quiz.e: Leaders like Malcolm X and Stokely Carmichael emphasized self-determination amid frustration with slow, incremental change.

quiz.q: Reaganomics primarily involved:
o: Higher tax rates on the wealthy and expanded spending on social programs
Large tax cuts, deregulation, and increased defense spending
Government control of prices and the breakup of large corporations
Large cuts in defense spending and a balanced federal budget
quiz.e: Reagan's supply-side economic policy combined tax cuts, deregulation, and a defense spending buildup.

quiz.q: Despite Reagan's small-government goals, his presidency saw:
o: A rapid fall in the national debt and lower federal spending overall
A sharp cut in military spending and the end of the federal deficit
A large tax increase that balanced the budget by the end of his term
Significant growth in the federal deficit and national debt
quiz.e: Tax cuts combined with increased defense spending led to substantially larger deficits and debt.

quiz.q: Gorbachev's policies of glasnost and perestroika were intended to:
o: Preserve communist rule by crushing dissent and expanding military control in Eastern Europe
Prepare the Soviet Union for a war against NATO by modernizing industry
Reform and open Soviet society/economy, but unintentionally hastened its collapse
Restore central planning and strengthen the Communist Party's grip on the economy
quiz.e: Gorbachev's reforms aimed to revitalize the USSR but instead accelerated its political and economic disintegration.

quiz.q: The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) symbolized:
o: The end of Soviet control over Eastern Europe
The beginning of Soviet expansion into Western Europe after World War II
The rise of a new American alliance with East Germany's leaders
The division of Germany into occupation zones by the Allied powers
quiz.e: The Wall's fall represented the collapse of Soviet influence in Eastern Europe, a key step toward the Cold War's end.

quiz.q: NAFTA (1994) established a free trade zone among:
o: The U.S., Canada, and Mexico
The U.S., China, and Japan
All members of the United Nations
The U.S. and the European Union
quiz.e: NAFTA created a trilateral free trade agreement among the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.

quiz.q: A major criticism of NAFTA and globalization was that they:
o: Raised wages for American factory workers and sped up growth in manufacturing
Caused a collapse in trade between the U.S. and Canada and Mexico
Contributed to outsourcing of manufacturing jobs overseas
Increased tariffs on imported goods and raised prices for American consumers
quiz.e: Critics argued free trade agreements like NAFTA accelerated the loss of U.S. manufacturing jobs to lower-wage countries.

quiz.q: The September 11, 2001 attacks directly led to:
o: The Iran hostage crisis and a new American alliance with Saudi Arabia
The War on Terror and the creation of the Department of Homeland Security
The collapse of the Soviet Union and an end to American military buildup
The invasion of Kuwait and the formation of a Gulf coalition
quiz.e: 9/11 prompted a major reorientation of U.S. foreign and domestic policy, including new homeland security institutions.

quiz.q: The USA PATRIOT Act, passed after 9/11, primarily:
o: Limited the government's power to monitor phone and email communications
Withdrew American troops from the Middle East and ended the Iraq War
Created a national identity card system and a federal ban on air travel
Expanded government surveillance and law enforcement powers to combat terrorism
quiz.e: The PATRIOT Act broadened federal surveillance and investigative powers in the name of counterterrorism.

quiz.q: The 2008 financial crisis was primarily rooted in:
o: A sudden collapse in oil prices and rising unemployment in the energy sector
The housing/mortgage market collapse and financial deregulation
Excessive government regulation of banks and limits on home lending
A stock market crash caused by speculation in internet and technology companies
quiz.e: Risky mortgage lending, complex financial instruments, and deregulation triggered the 2008 crisis and Great Recession.

quiz.q: The Affordable Care Act (2010) primarily aimed to:
o: Replace private insurance with a single government-run health plan for everyone
Expand health insurance coverage to more Americans
Cut Medicaid funding and shift health costs to individual states
Lower prescription drug prices by letting Medicare negotiate with manufacturers
quiz.e: The ACA sought to expand health coverage through insurance marketplaces, Medicaid expansion, and related reforms.

quiz.q: The Persian Gulf War (1991) demonstrated:
o: Post-Cold War U.S. military leadership in a coalition to expel Iraq from Kuwait
American reluctance to use force abroad without a clear threat to national security
The failure of the United Nations to organize a collective response to aggression
The Soviet Union's continued influence over Middle Eastern oil states
quiz.e: The U.S.-led coalition's swift victory in the Gulf War showcased America's post-Cold War global military role.

quiz.q: Deindustrialization in the late 20th century particularly affected which U.S. region?
o: The Sun Belt
The Rust Belt
The Pacific Northwest
New England exclusively
quiz.e: The 'Rust Belt' (Midwest/Northeast manufacturing centers) saw significant job losses as production shifted overseas.

quiz.q: Which best describes U.S. income inequality trends from the late 20th century onward?
o: Wages stagnated for many while wealth concentrated among high earners
Wages rose steadily for most workers while wealth spread more evenly across income groups
Income gaps narrowed as unions grew stronger and taxes on the rich increased
Middle-class earnings surged while the richest Americans saw their share decline
quiz.e: Despite economic growth, wage stagnation for many workers alongside wealth concentration widened income inequality.

quiz.q: The Soviet Union officially dissolved in:
quiz.e: The USSR formally dissolved in 1991, marking the definitive end of the Cold War and leaving the U.S. as the sole superpower.

quiz.q: The rise of the religious right (e.g., the Moral Majority) in the 1980s reflected:
o: A conservative political resurgence tied to religious activism
A decline of conservative influence as voters turned toward liberal social policies
A growing separation of religion and government supported by both parties
A reaction against Reagan's economic policies led by evangelical ministers
quiz.e: The Moral Majority and similar groups mobilized religious conservatives as a significant force within the Reagan-era conservative coalition.

quiz.q: The Columbian Exchange most dramatically affected Native American populations by:
o: introducing Old World diseases that caused catastrophic depopulation
bringing European crops that increased Native food supplies and population
introducing firearms that gave Native nations a military advantage over settlers
replacing Native farming with European-style plantations and a growing labor force
quiz.e: Smallpox and other diseases, to which Native peoples had no immunity, killed a large majority of the pre-contact population.

quiz.q: The Spanish encomienda system was primarily a means of:
o: extracting forced labor and tribute from Native communities
providing wages and farmland to Native families who converted to Christianity
protecting Native communities from raids by rival tribes and European pirates
organizing trade between Spanish merchants and Native artisans
quiz.e: Encomienda gave colonists the right to Native labor and tribute in exchange for nominal protection and Christianization.

quiz.q: Which Native society built large earthen mounds and supported a stratified urban center at Cahokia?
o: Mississippian
Pueblo
Iroquois
Inuit
quiz.e: Mississippian peoples used maize surpluses to sustain Cahokia, a large mound-building society near modern St. Louis.

quiz.q: European exploration of the Americas was driven above all by the search for:
o: new trade routes and sources of wealth (God, gold, glory)
religious freedom and the chance to build new Protestant communities
land for small farms and relief from overcrowding in European cities
a way to spread democracy and end the monarchies of Asia
quiz.e: The desire for a route to Asian markets and for gold and silver, alongside missionary and national rivalry, motivated exploration.

quiz.q: The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 demonstrated that:
o: Spanish rule over the region had remained unchallenged since conquest
Native peoples could organize sustained, effective resistance to Spanish rule
Native peoples had fully accepted Spanish religion and labor demands
the Spanish military had permanently lost control of the Southwest
quiz.e: Pueblo peoples drove the Spanish out of New Mexico for over a decade before Spain reconquered the region.

quiz.q: The Spanish casta system organized colonial society primarily by:
o: ancestry and place of birth
wealth alone
religious denomination
language spoken
quiz.e: The casta hierarchy ranked people from peninsulares and creoles down through mestizos, Native peoples, and Africans.

quiz.q: Compared with English colonization, Spanish colonization more often involved:
o: incorporating and converting large Native populations under colonial rule
forcing Native peoples off their land to create small independent farms
building self-governing communities with elected local assemblies
using indentured servants from Europe as the main source of labor
quiz.e: Spain conquered densely populated regions and ruled over Native labor, while English settlement tended to push Natives off the land.

quiz.q: The 'three sisters' agricultural system of many eastern Native peoples consisted of:
o: corn, beans, and squash
wheat, barley, and rye
tobacco, rice, and indigo
potatoes, tomatoes, and peppers
quiz.e: Corn, beans, and squash were grown together in a mutually supportive planting system.

quiz.q: Bartolome de las Casas is best known for:
o: condemning Spanish abuses of Native peoples
leading the conquest of the Aztecs
founding the first English colony
charting a westward route to Asia
quiz.e: Las Casas, a Dominican friar, publicized and denounced the brutality of the encomienda system.

quiz.q: Horses, pigs, and wheat moving from Europe to the Americas, and maize, potatoes, and tobacco moving the other way, are all examples of:
o: the Columbian Exchange
mercantile regulation
the Middle Passage
the headright system
quiz.e: The Columbian Exchange was the transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between hemispheres.

quiz.q: Pacific Northwest peoples such as the Chinook developed large, hierarchical, permanent villages primarily because of:
o: intensive corn cultivation and the use of irrigation canals
trade with European fur merchants and the arrival of horses
abundant salmon and other marine resources
control of mountain passes and large-scale buffalo hunting
quiz.e: Rich, reliable fishing allowed dense, socially complex, sedentary communities without farming.

quiz.q: The primary goal of the Spanish mission system was to:
o: set up elected town councils and teach Native peoples self-government
convert Native peoples to Catholicism and organize their labor
collect furs and tribute for the Crown and guard the frontier
protect Native lands from settlers and preserve traditional beliefs
quiz.e: Missions concentrated Native populations for religious conversion and controlled labor.

quiz.q: West African societies at the time of early European contact were:
o: isolated farming villages with no trade and a single common language
small nomadic bands without metalworking or organized political leadership
ruled by one large empire that controlled the entire coast and interior
organized into a range of states and kingdoms with established trade networks
quiz.e: Kingdoms such as Songhai, Benin, and Kongo had complex political and commercial systems well before European contact.

quiz.q: The Virginia colony became economically viable after 1612 primarily through the cultivation of:
o: tobacco
rice
sugar
cotton
quiz.e: John Rolfe's tobacco gave the Chesapeake a profitable cash crop and drove demand for labor and land.

quiz.q: The Massachusetts Bay Colony was founded chiefly as:
o: a Puritan religious community and 'city upon a hill'
a commercial venture designed to ship furs and timber to English merchants
a refuge for persecuted English Catholics under a proprietary charter
a military colony meant to defend against the French and Spanish
quiz.e: Puritans led by John Winthrop sought to build a model godly society.

quiz.q: The headright system in the Chesapeake:
o: required planters to educate and free indentured servants after seven years
granted land to those who paid for their own or others' passage
gave every colonist an equal share of land owned in common by the colony
taxed tobacco exports to pay for defense against Native raids
quiz.e: Headrights of roughly 50 acres per person imported encouraged wealthy planters to import laborers and accumulate land.

quiz.q: Bacon's Rebellion (1676) is often seen as a turning point because it:
o: ended the use of enslaved labor and freed indentured servants in Virginia
united small farmers and wealthy planters under a new colonial government
ended royal rule in Virginia and created an elected colonial legislature
accelerated the shift from indentured servitude to racial slavery
quiz.e: Fear of armed, landless former servants pushed planters toward enslaved African labor, which was permanent and racially controlled.

quiz.q: The Maryland Act of Toleration (1649) protected:
o: all believers, including Jews and Quakers, with full political rights
Trinitarian Christians, especially Catholics
Anglicans only, as the established Church of the colony
Protestants who refused to accept any form of church hierarchy
quiz.e: It guaranteed freedom of worship to Christians who accepted the Trinity, largely to protect the Catholic minority.

quiz.q: Compared with the Chesapeake, early New England had:
o: shorter life expectancy, more men than women, and weaker family structures
a large population of enslaved Africans working on cash-crop farms
longer life expectancy, more balanced sex ratios, and stronger family structures
a legal ban on religious dissent and a heavy reliance on indentured servants
quiz.e: Healthier conditions and family migration produced more stable, town-centered communities in New England.

quiz.q: Mercantilism held that a colony's role was to:
o: buy raw materials from foreign nations and export finished goods to rival powers
build local industries and sell manufactured goods to other European markets
operate independently of the mother country under their own trade laws
enrich the mother country by supplying raw materials and buying finished goods
quiz.e: Under mercantilism, colonies existed to strengthen the imperial economy, regulated by acts like the Navigation Acts.

quiz.q: The Navigation Acts required that:
o: colonial assemblies approve all taxes before they could be collected
colonial trade in key goods be carried on English ships through English ports
colonial courts try British officials accused of crimes by juries of colonists
colonists be barred from settling on lands west of the mountains
quiz.e: The acts channeled 'enumerated' colonial goods through England to benefit English merchants and the crown.

quiz.q: The First Great Awakening contributed to the coming Revolution by:
o: strengthening the authority of ministers and church hierarchy over colonial life
turning colonists toward reason and science instead of religious revival
convincing colonists that Parliament had the right to regulate religious life
encouraging colonists to question established authority
quiz.e: Revivalist challenges to religious hierarchy fostered a broader willingness to question authority.

quiz.q: The 'middle passage' refers to:
o: the trade route linking New England rum producers to West African markets
the second stage of the voyage carrying sugar from the Caribbean to England
the forced ocean voyage of enslaved Africans to the Americas
the overland journey of captured Africans from the interior to the coast
quiz.e: It was the brutal Atlantic leg of the triangular trade carrying captive Africans to slavery.

quiz.q: The Middle Colonies (Pennsylvania, New York, New Jersey) were notable for:
o: ethnic and religious diversity and mixed farming
a rigid Puritan establishment
near-total reliance on plantation agriculture
the absence of any European settlement
quiz.e: They attracted varied groups (Quakers, Germans, Dutch, Scots-Irish) and grew grain for export.

quiz.q: The Salem witch trials (1692) are often interpreted as a symptom of:
o: a genuine religious revival that spread through New England's towns
social strain, factionalism, and anxiety in a changing Puritan society
a political crisis caused by royal interference in colonial government
a conflict between Puritans and Native Americans over land and trade
quiz.e: Historians link the accusations to community tensions, gender norms, and frontier insecurity.

quiz.q: Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson were both:
o: leaders of Puritan congregations who held high office in the colony
religious dissenters banished from Massachusetts Bay
Native American converts who preached against colonial expansion
Anglican missionaries who criticized Puritan rule from England
quiz.e: Williams (founder of Rhode Island) and Hutchinson challenged Puritan orthodoxy and were expelled.

quiz.q: The Stamp Act (1765) provoked especially fierce resistance because it was:
o: an external duty on imported goods that affected only merchants and shippers
a tax collected only on luxury goods and paid mostly by wealthy planters
a direct internal tax on printed materials affecting many colonists
a levy imposed by colonial assemblies to pay for local defense
quiz.e: As an internal revenue tax touching newspapers, contracts, and licenses, it galvanized broad opposition and the cry of 'no taxation without representation'.

quiz.q: Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776) argued that:
o: the colonies were too weak and divided to survive without British protection
monarchy was the best form of government and should be reformed rather than abolished
Britain would soon repeal its taxes if the colonies remained loyal and peaceful
it was absurd for a continent to be ruled by an island, and independence was the logical course
quiz.e: Paine made a plain-language case for immediate independence and republican government.

quiz.q: The most important weakness of the Articles of Confederation was that Congress could not:
o: set up a national post office or settle disputes between states
make treaties with foreign nations or declare war on other countries
borrow money from foreign governments or print paper currency
levy taxes or regulate interstate and foreign commerce
quiz.e: Without taxing or commerce power, the national government could not pay debts or manage trade disputes.

quiz.q: Shays's Rebellion (1786-87) influenced the movement for a new constitution by:
o: showing that state governments were strong enough to handle rebellions on their own
convincing leaders that a larger Congress was needed to regulate the militia
proving that farmers should have a larger voice in the new government
highlighting the national government's inability to maintain order and address economic distress
quiz.e: An armed uprising of indebted Massachusetts farmers alarmed elites and boosted support for a stronger central government.

quiz.q: The Great (Connecticut) Compromise at the Constitutional Convention resolved the dispute over:
o: representation, by creating a bicameral legislature
slavery, by counting each enslaved person as three-fifths of a free person
the powers of the executive, by creating a single president elected by Congress
the national debt, by having the federal government assume state war debts
quiz.e: It paired a House based on population with a Senate giving each state equal representation.

quiz.q: The Three-Fifths Compromise determined that enslaved people would be counted as three-fifths of a person for purposes of:
o: both voting eligibility in federal elections and military conscription quotas
only the allocation of federal land grants and western territorial seats
both representation in the House and direct taxation
both the length of presidential terms and state militia funding
quiz.e: It boosted southern representation while also apportioning some federal taxes.

quiz.q: Anti-Federalists opposed ratification of the Constitution mainly because they feared:
o: a strong central government that lacked a bill of rights
a weak central government that left the states too powerful to unify
a federal system that banned slavery and angered the southern states
an executive branch that was too weak to enforce laws or defend the nation
quiz.e: They demanded explicit protection of individual liberties, leading to the Bill of Rights.

quiz.q: Hamilton's financial program included all of the following EXCEPT:
o: immediate abolition of the national debt through repudiation
gradual refunding of the national debt by cutting all tariffs on imports
creation of a national bank to stabilize the currency and handle federal funds
federal assumption of state war debts to bind creditors to the new government
quiz.e: Hamilton wanted to fund the debt at face value to build credit, not repudiate it.

quiz.q: Washington's Farewell Address warned against:
o: entangling trade agreements and the growth of a large permanent navy
a national bank and the growth of federal power over the western lands
foreign immigration and the spread of political clubs favoring France
permanent foreign alliances and the spirit of party (faction)
quiz.e: He cautioned against entangling alliances and the divisive effects of political factions.

quiz.q: The Whiskey Rebellion (1794) was significant because the federal government:
o: was forced to repeal the whiskey excise after armed resistance in Pennsylvania
demonstrated its power to enforce its laws, unlike under the Articles
showed that the army could not be raised without state militia approval
lost the support of western farmers, who then allied with Spain over trade
quiz.e: Washington led troops to suppress resistance to the whiskey excise, showing the new government's strength.

quiz.q: The XYZ Affair (1797-98) worsened relations with:
o: France
Britain
Spain
the Barbary States
quiz.e: French agents' demand for bribes to open negotiations outraged Americans and led to the undeclared Quasi-War.

quiz.q: The Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions (1798-99) advanced the theory that:
o: the federal courts alone could decide whether acts of Congress were constitutional
the president could ignore laws passed by Congress during wartime
states could judge the constitutionality of federal laws (nullification)
Congress could suspend the Bill of Rights for foreign-born residents
quiz.e: Written by Madison and Jefferson against the Alien and Sedition Acts, they asserted a state role in checking federal power.

quiz.q: The 'corrupt bargain' of 1824 refers to the belief that:
o: Andrew Jackson paid several state electors to switch their votes to Adams in exchange for a cabinet seat
the Bank of the United States financed Adams in exchange for a renewed charter from Congress
Henry Clay threw House support to John Quincy Adams in exchange for becoming Secretary of State
Congress ignored the Electoral College and gave the presidency to the candidate with the most popular votes
quiz.e: Jackson supporters charged that Clay's backing of Adams, followed by Clay's appointment, was a corrupt deal.

quiz.q: The Indian Removal Act (1830) and the resulting Trail of Tears involved:
o: the voluntary migration of southeastern tribes west after fair land-exchange treaties
a Supreme Court order protecting Cherokee lands that Jackson enforced with federal troops
the peaceful sale of tribal lands to Georgia and Alabama at fair market prices
the forced relocation of southeastern Native nations west of the Mississippi
quiz.e: Despite Worcester v. Georgia, the Cherokee and others were driven west, with thousands dying en route.

quiz.q: The Nullification Crisis (1832-33) arose when South Carolina attempted to:
o: secede from the Union and form a separate southern government over slavery
close the state's ports to all foreign trade and abolish the national bank
declare a federal tariff null and void within the state
refuse to send troops to a federal army during a war
quiz.e: South Carolina claimed the power to void the 'Tariff of Abominations'; Jackson threatened force and a compromise tariff resolved it.

quiz.q: Jackson's veto of the Second Bank of the United States charter was based on the argument that the Bank:
o: was constitutional but charged farmers too little interest on their loans
was controlled by federal judges who used it to punish his political allies
printed too little paper money to meet the needs of western settlers
was unconstitutional and served wealthy, often foreign, elites
quiz.e: Jackson portrayed the Bank as a privileged 'monster' hostile to the common man.

quiz.q: The Market Revolution was driven above all by improvements in:
o: the invention of the cotton gin and the growth of southern plantation slavery
transportation and communication (canals, roads, railroads, telegraph)
heavy foreign investment from Britain in American banks and factories
federal land grants and public subsidies that financed western family farms
quiz.e: Faster, cheaper movement of goods and information integrated regional economies into a national market.

quiz.q: The Lowell system of textile manufacturing initially relied on the labor of:
o: young unmarried New England women
enslaved people from the South
Irish immigrant men
child apprentices from England
quiz.e: Early Lowell mills recruited farm daughters who lived in company boardinghouses.

quiz.q: The Second Great Awakening fueled which set of reform movements?
o: temperance, abolition, women's rights, and asylum/prison reform
free trade, lower tariffs, westward removal of tribes, and expansion of the banking system
nativism, Indian removal, slavery expansion, and a stronger national bank
internal improvements, tariff protection, free-silver coinage, and railroad subsidies
quiz.e: Revivalist belief in human perfectibility inspired a wide range of moral reform campaigns.

quiz.q: The Seneca Falls Convention (1848) produced the Declaration of Sentiments, which demanded:
o: equal rights for women, including suffrage
immediate abolition of slavery only
temperance legislation
free public education
quiz.e: Modeled on the Declaration of Independence, it called for women's equality and the vote.

quiz.q: 'Manifest Destiny' was the belief that:
o: the North and South would always share equal power in the Senate and House
the United States was destined to expand across the continent
industrial growth and factory production would inevitably transform the country
slavery would fade away on its own as the country expanded westward
quiz.e: The phrase justified territorial expansion as a national and providential mission.

quiz.q: The Missouri Compromise (1820):
o: admitted Missouri as a slave state, Maine as free, and banned slavery north of 36 degrees 30 minutes
admitted Maine as a slave state, Missouri as free, and banned slavery south of 36 degrees 30 minutes
abolished the slave trade in Washington, D.C. and let popular sovereignty decide all new territories
admitted Missouri as free and Texas as slave while repealing the Northwest Ordinance
quiz.e: It preserved the balance of slave and free states and drew a line across the Louisiana Territory.

quiz.q: The 'gag rule' in the House of Representatives (1836-1844):
o: banned all debate on the tariff and bank issues without any vote in Congress
required a two-thirds vote before Congress could declare war or ratify treaties
prohibited members from criticizing the president or the Supreme Court
automatically tabled antislavery petitions without debate
quiz.e: It suppressed abolitionist petitions and was fought by John Quincy Adams as a free-speech issue.

quiz.q: By the 1830s many white southerners defended slavery as:
o: a 'positive good' rather than a 'necessary evil'
a temporary institution soon to be abolished
incompatible with Christianity
economically unimportant
quiz.e: Figures like John C. Calhoun reframed slavery as beneficial to both races and society.

quiz.q: The Compromise of 1850 included which provision that most inflamed the North?
o: a stricter Fugitive Slave Act
the admission of California as a slave state
a ban on slavery in Utah
the abolition of the slave trade in all southern states
quiz.e: The new Fugitive Slave Act compelled northern cooperation in returning escapees, radicalizing opinion.

quiz.q: The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854):
o: admitted Kansas as a free state and Nebraska as a slave state under the old line
banned slavery in all western territories and strengthened the Missouri Compromise
created the Republican Party by law and ended the Whig Party in Congress
repealed the Missouri Compromise line and applied popular sovereignty
quiz.e: By opening territory north of 36 degrees 30 minutes to possible slavery, it triggered 'Bleeding Kansas' and party realignment.

quiz.q: In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) the Supreme Court held that:
o: enslaved people who lived on free soil became free and could sue as citizens
the Missouri Compromise was constitutional and Congress could ban slavery in the territories
Black people were not citizens and Congress could not bar slavery from the territories
popular sovereignty was illegal, but free Black people were citizens in the North
quiz.e: Chief Justice Taney's opinion denied Black citizenship and struck down federal restriction of slavery in the territories.

quiz.q: The Republican Party, founded in 1854, was united primarily by opposition to:
o: the expansion of slavery into the territories
immigration from Ireland and Germany
protective tariffs
the national bank
quiz.e: Republicans were a free-soil coalition, not (mostly) abolitionists, focused on stopping slavery's spread.

quiz.q: Lincoln justified the Emancipation Proclamation (1863) primarily as:
o: a war measure to weaken the Confederacy
a fulfillment of the original Constitution
a response to a Supreme Court ruling
a treaty obligation with Britain
quiz.e: It freed enslaved people in areas in rebellion, targeting the Confederate war effort and permitting Black enlistment.

quiz.q: During the Civil War the Union Congress passed all of the following EXCEPT:
o: the repeal of the tariff
the Homestead Act
the Pacific Railway Act
the Morrill Land-Grant College Act
quiz.e: With southern Democrats absent, Republicans enacted a nationalist economic program, including a higher tariff.

quiz.q: The New York City draft riots of 1863 were fueled largely by:
o: opposition by Southern planters to the Emancipation Proclamation and the end of slavery
fear of a Confederate invasion and outrage that Lincoln suspended habeas corpus
a long labor dispute in the city's shipyards and anger at low wages and rising prices
working-class resentment that the wealthy could buy exemptions and anger over fighting to free enslaved people
quiz.e: Irish and other workers attacked draft offices and Black residents, resenting the $300 commutation fee and emancipation.

quiz.q: The Reconstruction Amendments accomplished which of the following?
o: gave women the vote, created a federal income tax, and limited presidents to two terms
abolished slavery, granted citizenship and equal protection, and barred racial denial of the vote
abolished slavery, set up a federal income tax, and guaranteed free public education
ended slavery, gave women suffrage, and created the Freedmen's Bureau
quiz.e: The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments, respectively, achieved these goals (though enforcement soon lapsed in the South).

quiz.q: The Freedmen's Bureau primarily provided:
o: permanent 40-acre land grants, military governance, and reparations paid by former enslavers
food, schools, and legal aid to formerly enslaved people and poor whites
federal troops, voting registration, and permanent pensions to former Union soldiers
cash payments, mule loans, and land redistribution from rebels to every freedman
quiz.e: It offered relief and education but had limited resources and was dismantled by 1872.

quiz.q: Radical Reconstruction (Congressional Reconstruction) featured:
o: a lenient plan that pardoned most Confederates and restored their prewar state governments quickly
military districts in the South and requirements to ratify the 14th Amendment for readmission
immediate readmission of southern states with no requirements for ratifying new amendments
an end of federal involvement in the South and white southern control of state governments
quiz.e: Congress overrode Johnson, divided the South into five military districts, and set conditions for readmission.

quiz.q: 'Redeemer' governments that took power in the South after Reconstruction generally:
o: expanded public schools, raised taxes, and supported continued Black officeholding
backed high tariffs, industrial subsidies, and continued federal supervision of elections
cut spending, rolled back Black political power, and entrenched white Democratic rule
welcomed Northern troops, protected Black voters, and funded new railroad construction
quiz.e: Redeemers dismantled Reconstruction reforms and began the long move toward disenfranchisement and Jim Crow.

quiz.q: Vertical integration, as practiced by Andrew Carnegie in steel, means:
o: buying out competing steel firms to dominate one stage of the industry
fixing prices and dividing markets with rival steel makers through secret agreements
controlling every stage of production from raw materials to finished product
selling company stock to the public and sharing control with many investors
quiz.e: Carnegie owned mines, ships, railroads, and mills, controlling the whole supply chain.

quiz.q: John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil is the classic example of:
o: horizontal integration (dominating one stage of an industry)
vertical integration (controlling every stage from raw materials to product)
government ownership of the oil industry under a public regulatory board
a worker-owned cooperative sharing profits among refinery employees
quiz.e: Standard Oil absorbed or destroyed competing refiners to control refining, then used a trust structure.

quiz.q: The 'Gospel of Wealth' argued by Andrew Carnegie held that:
o: the rich had a duty to use their fortunes for the public good
poverty was a sign of moral failure that should not be relieved
government should redistribute wealth
labor unions were essential to fairness
quiz.e: Carnegie urged wealthy men to act as trustees of their money, funding libraries and education.

quiz.q: Social Darwinism was used in the Gilded Age to:
o: support strong antitrust laws and government regulation of business power
promote labor unions and demand higher wages and a shorter working day
defend Native land rights and criticize the spread of industrial wealth
justify laissez-faire economics and great inequality as natural
quiz.e: Thinkers applied 'survival of the fittest' to society, opposing aid to the poor and regulation of business.

quiz.q: The Haymarket affair (1886) damaged the labor movement because:
o: it revealed that employers had infiltrated unions and caused the violence themselves
a bombing at a Chicago rally linked unions in the public mind with violence and anarchism
the Knights of Labor won their demands and then voluntarily dissolved their organization
the government legalized all strikes, which led employers to unite against unions
quiz.e: After the bomb killed police, a backlash weakened the Knights of Labor and broad labor organizing.

quiz.q: The Homestead Strike (1892) and Pullman Strike (1894) both ended with:
o: union victories and employer recognition of collective bargaining rights
binding government arbitration that settled the wage disputes fairly
the use of state or federal force to break the strike
the bankruptcy of the employers and the takeover of their plants by workers
quiz.e: Troops and injunctions crushed both strikes, showing government's pro-management stance.

quiz.q: 'New' immigrants of the 1880s-1900s came predominantly from:
o: southern and eastern Europe
northern and western Europe
East Asia
Latin America
quiz.e: Italians, Poles, Russian Jews, and others arrived in large numbers, prompting nativist reactions.

quiz.q: The Populist (People's) Party's Omaha Platform (1892) called for all of the following EXCEPT:
o: a return to a strict gold standard
free and unlimited coinage of silver
a graduated income tax
government ownership of railroads and telegraphs
quiz.e: Populists wanted inflationary 'free silver,' not a tighter gold standard.

quiz.q: The election of 1896, in which William McKinley defeated William Jennings Bryan, is often seen as:
o: a triumph for the free-silver movement and the rise of Populist power in Washington
the first presidential election in history decided by a vote in the House
a victory for the labor vote and urban workers over Eastern banking interests
the end of Populism as a national force and the start of Republican dominance
quiz.e: Bryan's loss ended the agrarian revolt's momentum and began a long period of GOP power.

quiz.q: Sharecropping in the postwar South:
o: kept many Black and poor white families in cycles of debt and dependency
gave freed people full ownership of the land they farmed after a few years
was quickly replaced by wage labor as Black families moved to northern cities
was outlawed by the Freedmen's Bureau and replaced by federal land grants
quiz.e: The crop-lien system tied tenants to landowners and merchants through perpetual debt.

quiz.q: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) established the constitutional doctrine of:
o: 'separate but equal'
'one person, one vote'
'clear and present danger'
'substantive due process' for corporations
quiz.e: The Court upheld a Louisiana law segregating railroad cars, legitimizing Jim Crow for decades.

quiz.q: Muckrakers such as Upton Sinclair and Ida Tarbell were:
o: leaders of the Socialist Party who organized labor strikes against industries
corporate public-relations writers who defended large business trusts to the public
officials in Theodore Roosevelt's administration who enforced antitrust laws
investigative journalists who exposed corruption and abuses
